segments.he: סעיף ה עמ"ש הגאון אמוז"ל בסק"ד על הש"ך בסקכ"ו דהעלה אם ראתה אשה ר"ח שבט אדר ניסן ואח"כ סירג' וראתה סיון ואח"כ אב דחשבינן ניסן לוסת הקבוע ואין כאן רק ב"פ לסירוג והק' ז"ל הא בגמ' דב"ק בעי' לי' שור נגח ה' ו' שבת שבת ושבת שבת קמיית' ליומא קמא שדינן ואייעד לכולא יומא או לשבת בתריית' שדינן ולא אייעד אלא לשבתות ועלתה בתיקו וכן הרמב"ם פ"ו מנ"מ כתב דהוא ספק וא"כ הדברים דומים בלי הבדל כלל וא"א בתיקו במלתא דרבנן ספיקא לקולא א"כ יש לילך לקולא לכל צד ולומר דקבעה וסת לסירוג ולא לחודש וא"צ לחוש אלא מב' לב' חדשים וכו' ע"ש וטרם אעלה אמרתי להתבונן אם יש נ"מ לדינא לדברי הש"ך דהחמיר ולדברי אמו"ז הגז"ל דהוכיח להקל כי לכאורה העיקר פלפול בהך נדון אשה שראתה שבט אדר ניסן ואח"כ סיון אב א"כ כל הספק אם הגיע לחודש אלול אי כדברי הש"ך דשדינן ניסן לוסת החודש א"כ אסור' אלול מכח וסת החודש דלא דלגה רק ב"פ וא"א כדברי אמוז"ל דשדינן ניסן לוסת הסירוג לקולא א"כ יהיה ר"ח מותרת אבל יותר לכאורה אין נ"מ דממנ"פ אם רואה באלול איגלאי מילתא דבוסת החודש קיימא דהא כל סברתו להתיר מכח ספק והשתא ע"י ראית אלול אתברר לנו דבוסת קמיית' קיימא דשכיח וכרוב נשים חזית וא"כ הספק רק על אלול ואף כי צעיר ישראל לימים ולחכמה ואיני כדאי להכניס ראשי בין שני הרים גדולים מ"מ לעצור במילין מי יכול אמרתי לכאורה כ"ע מודה דאסור' באלול דאף דאזלינן לקולא שקבעה וסת לסירוג כדברי אמו"ז הגז"ל דכבר הבאתי בס"ק הקודם דברי הרמב"ם בפ"ח מהא"ב דפסק דאף דוודאי תקבע וסת הדילוג דמ"מ חוששת לחודש הבא אולי תקבע וסת החודש ולעיל הק' הג' אמוז"ל על המחבר למה השמיט דעת הרמב"ם דכן הוא דעת התו' וא"א כמש"ל דרמב"ם איירי בספק קביעות וסת לדילג ולזה כ"ע מודה א"כ גם כאן דאיכא ספק' טובי ובאת להתיר רק מכח ספיק' לקולא פשיטא דצריך לחוש ופשיט' אם הרמב"ם איירי בוסת הדילוג גמור א"כ כאן דאיכא ספק טובי כ"ע מודה לדינא דרמב"ם ותוס' דאסור' לעולם בר"ח אלול הבא א"כ ברור דאסור' באלול הבא ובאלול אתברר לנו הספק אך באמת ק' על הש"ך מנ"מ אם שדינן ניסן לוסת החודש הקבוע או לא דהא לפ"ד הנ"ל ר"ח אלול לעולם אסורה לשמש ובהגיע תור אלול אתברר לנו הספק וא"ל אם לא שדינן ניסן לוסת החודש הקבוע ס"ל להש"ך דגם לוסת הסירוג לא שדינן רק הוי כאשה שאין לה וסת כלל וצריך בדיקה לפני תשמיש וכה"ג צריך לחוש להפלגה וכדומה חדא זה דוחק וחומר' יתיר' דהא ודאי אית לה וסת או חודש או דילוג ובלא"ה בזה ודאי אזלינן לקולא ועוד לדברי הש"ך סקפ"ד דס"ל אפי' אשה שאין לה וסת תוך למ"ד הוי כאשה שיש לה וסת וא"צ בדיקה לבעלה ובלמ"ד נתברר לנו הספק כנ"ל וא"ל אף דאלול באסור' קיימא מחמת חשש דלמא תקבע וסת החודש מ"מ סמוך לוסתה מותרת ואינה אסורה רק אותה עונה ממש משא"כ אם אסורה מחמת וסת קבוע אסורה לשמש אפי' סמוך לוסתה הא מבואר לעיל בסקפ"ד שצריך לפרוש סמוך לוסת' אפי' לא ראתה רק פ"א ודוחק לחלק דכ"ז אם אותו ראיה מקדם אין לתלות כלל בוסת אחר אבל במקום ספק יוכל לומר שזה הראי' היה וסת דילוג ואף דניחוש אולי היה לקביעות אחר אז א"צ סמוך לוסתה לפרוש כיון דבלא"ה הוא רק דרבנן וספיק' לקולא זה דוחק גדול וצ"ל בדוחק דוודאי א"א כדעת הש"ך דהוי קבוע א"כ בעברה וסתה אסור לבוא עלי' בלי שאלת פי' כמבואר לעיל בסי' קפ"ד דלא כהרי"ף ורמב"ם דמתירין לבוא עלי' אפי' ישינה משא"כ אם הוא רק מחמת חשש כ"ע מודה לדינא דרמב"ם והרי"ף דמותר לבוא עלי' אפי' ישינה דהוי בכלל ס"ס אולי ניסן שדינן לוסת דילוג ואין זמנ' לראות ואת"ל לוסת חודש שדינן מ"מ אולי לא ראתה ומותרת וזה יהיה כוונת אמו"ז הגאון זצ"ל אבל בגוף הדין אין כאן נ"מ דבר"ח אלול ודאי אסורה דלמא לא נחוש בספק וסת דילוג מה שהרמב"ם ותוס' חוששין אפילו בלי ספק כלל ובהגיע תור אלול נתברר לנו הספק דודאי אם ראתה חזינן דוסת החודש קבעה לוסת ואם לא ראתה פשיטא דקבעה וסת לדילוג וצ"ל דכל ההפרש הוא אם בעלה צריך לשאול אותה או מותר לבוא עלי' בלי שאלת פי' כדעת הרי"ף והרמב"ם וזה יהי' כוונת הש"ך דכתב בפשיטות דניסן לוסת החודש שדינן וא"כ אסורה ותמה עליה הא הוא עלתה בתיקו וספיק' לקולא וא"כ א"צ לחוש רק מב' לב' חדשים וא"כ פשיטא דמותר לבוא עלי' בלי שאלת פי' בעברה עונת אלול אבל בגוף הדין דר"ח אלול אסור' לשמש גם אמוז"ל מודה זד"ג אך י"ל דאיכא נ"מ טובא בניהם לענין עקיר' ודאי אם לא ראתה בר"ח אלול הבע"ל מותרת מ"מ אם תראה אח"כ כ' תשרי ובר"ח תשרי לא ראתה לדעת הש"ך עדיין יש לה וסת קבוע לר"ח דהא לא עקרה עדיין ג"פ כסדרן ולדעת אמו"ז הגאון ז"ל א"צ עקיר' כלל לוסת החודש וצריך עקיר' ג"פ לוסת הסירוג דקבעה וצ"ע כי יש לדחות גם זה:
segments.en: Seif 5. Regarding what my grandfather, the Gaon of blessed memory, wrote in seif katan 4 on Shach, seif katan 26: the Shach concludes that if a woman saw on Rosh Chodesh of Shevat, Adar, and Nisan, and afterward skipped a month and saw in Sivan and then Av, we assign the Nisan sighting to the established monthly veset, so there are only two instances of an alternating-month veset. My grandfather challenged this from Bava Kamma, where the Gemara asks concerning an ox that gored on Thursday, Friday, Shabbos, Shabbos, and Shabbos: do we assign the first Shabbos to the first sequence, so that it became forewarned for all days, or to the later Shabbos sequence, so that it became forewarned only for Shabbos? The question remains unresolved, and Rambam in chapter 6 of Hilchos Nizkei Mamon likewise rules that it is doubtful. If so, the cases appear completely parallel. Since the question remains unresolved and a veset is a rabbinic matter, the doubt should be resolved leniently in every direction, assigning Nisan to the alternating veset rather than the monthly veset, so that she need be concerned only every second month. See there. Before addressing the substance, I wished to consider whether there is any practical difference between the Shach's stringent view and my grandfather's proof for leniency. In the case of a woman who saw in Shevat, Adar, Nisan, then Sivan and Av, the immediate uncertainty concerns Rosh Chodesh Elul. According to the Shach, since Nisan belongs to the fixed monthly veset, she is prohibited in Elul because that monthly veset has been skipped only twice. According to my grandfather, if we leniently assign Nisan to the alternating pattern, Rosh Chodesh Elul would be permitted. Beyond that, however, there initially seems to be no practical difference, because if she sees in Elul it becomes clear that she remained with the monthly veset. His entire basis for leniency was doubt; once she sees in Elul, the matter is clarified in favor of the earlier, more common monthly pattern. Thus the doubt would concern only Elul itself. Although I am young in years and wisdom and unfit to place my head between two great mountains, I cannot refrain from speaking. It appears that everyone should agree that she is prohibited in Elul. Even if we rule leniently that she established an alternating veset, as my grandfather says, I already cited in the preceding seif katan Rambam in chapter 8 of Hilchos Issurei Biah, who rules that even when she certainly establishes a progressively changing veset, she must nevertheless be concerned for the next month lest she establish a monthly veset. My grandfather himself earlier asked why the Mechaber omitted Rambam's view, which is also Tosafos's view. If, as explained there, Rambam deals even with a doubtful establishment of a changing veset and everyone agrees to that concern, then here too, where there are multiple doubts and the proposed leniency rests only on doubt, she certainly must be concerned. If Rambam deals with a fully established changing veset, all the more so here, where there are added doubts, everyone should agree with Rambam and Tosafos that she is prohibited on the coming Rosh Chodesh Elul. Thus it is clear that she is prohibited in Elul, and in Elul the doubt will be clarified. The difficulty against the Shach is then what practical difference it makes whether we assign Nisan to the established monthly veset. According to what I have said, Rosh Chodesh Elul is forbidden in any event, and when Elul arrives the doubt will be clarified. One cannot say that if Nisan is not assigned to the established monthly veset, the Shach holds it is also not assigned to the alternating veset, leaving her as a woman with no veset who requires examination before relations and concern for intervals and the like. That would be strained and excessively stringent: she certainly has either a monthly or alternating veset, and in such a doubt we certainly rule leniently. Moreover, according to the Shach in siman 184, even a woman without a fixed veset, within 30 days, is treated like a woman with a veset and does not require examination for her husband; by day 30 the doubt will have been clarified. Nor can one say that although Elul is forbidden because she might establish the monthly veset, she may have relations close to her expected veset and is prohibited only during the actual onah, whereas if the veset is already fixed she is prohibited even near it. Above in siman 184 it is explained that one must separate near the veset even after a single prior sighting. It would be very forced to distinguish that this applies only when the prior sighting cannot be attributed to another veset, whereas in a doubtful case we might assign it to the alternating veset and, although we remain concerned that it might belong to another pattern, not require separation near the veset because the entire matter is rabbinic and a doubt is lenient. One must therefore say, with difficulty, that according to the Shach, who definitely assigns Nisan to the fixed veset, once the time passes she may not have relations without expressly asking her, as explained above in siman 184, unlike the Rif and Rambam, who permit relations even if she is asleep. If the monthly veset is only a concern, however, everyone agrees with Rambam and Rif that after the time passes he may have relations with her even while she sleeps, because there is a double doubt: perhaps Nisan belongs to the alternating veset and it is not her time to see, and even if Nisan belongs to the monthly veset, perhaps she did not see. This may be my grandfather's intention. Still, with respect to the basic prohibition on Rosh Chodesh Elul there is no difference, for even my grandfather agrees she is forbidden then. It is impossible to ignore the possible alternating veset when Rambam and Tosafos are stringent even without such uncertainty. When Elul arrives, the doubt is clarified: if she sees, we see that she established the monthly veset; if she does not see, it is clear that she established the alternating veset. Thus the difference is whether her husband must ask her explicitly after the Elul onah, or may have relations without asking, according to Rif and Rambam. This would explain why Shach says simply that Nisan is assigned to the monthly veset and therefore she is prohibited, while my grandfather objects that the Gemara leaves the analogous question unresolved and a rabbinic doubt is lenient, so she need be concerned only every second month, meaning that after the Elul onah has passed her husband may have relations without explicitly asking. As to the prohibition on Rosh Chodesh Elul itself, my grandfather likewise agrees. There may, however, be a substantial practical difference concerning uprooting the veset. If she did not see on Rosh Chodesh Elul, she is certainly permitted afterward. Yet if she then sees on the twentieth of Tishrei and does not see on Rosh Chodesh Tishrei, according to the Shach she still has a fixed Rosh Chodesh veset, because she has not yet uprooted it three consecutive times. According to my grandfather, the monthly veset requires no uprooting at all, while the alternating veset that she established would require three occasions of uprooting. This too requires study, because it may be rejected.

segments.he: אמנם בגוף הקו' נראה להליץ בעד הגאון הש"ך דלכאורה קו' אמו"ז הגז"ל קשה ביותר על הגמ' ב"ק ותפשוט מסוגיא דנדה כי לכאורה דברי הש"ך מבוארים מגמ' וכאשר אבאר דאי' שם ב"ק דף ל"ד אבעי להו שור שנגח שבת שבת ושבת יום א' וב' מהו שבת בתריית' לשבת שדינן ואייעד לשבתות ולא לימי חול א"ד בתר שני ימים אחר שבת שדינן ואייעד לכולא יומא נגח בה' ובו' שבת שבת וכו' שבת קמיית' וכו' והנה לכאורה קשה הא הגמ' מדמי נגיחות לפלוגת' דרב ושמואל בוסת והא אי' בנדה דף ס"ד אתיבי' היתה למודה לראות בט"ו ושינת' לט"ז וכו' שינת' לי"ז וכו' שינתה לי"ח הותרו כולן ואינו נאסרה אלא מי"ח ואילך וק' לרב א"ל רב למודה שאני ופי' רש"י ודאי למודה לראות בט"ו ראיות ט"ו שדינין לט"ו הקודמים כי קאמרינן אלא אם התחילה לראות או באשה שאין לה וסת עכ"ל א"כ לפ"ז אם ראתה אשה ב"פ בט"ו לחודש והיום ראתה בט"ו דקבעה בה וסת דא"צ יותר מג"פ ושינת' אח"כ לט"ז ואח"כ לי"ז מודה רב דצריך עוד דילוג לח"י כמבואר ברש"י דראי' ט"ו שדינן לוסת קבוע רק הוא אומר דסגי בב' דילוגים היינו אם התחילה לראות אבל לא אם תשליש היום בראי' ט"ו הזה לוסת קבוע א"כ מ"פ הגמ' גבי נגיחות נגח ה' ו' שבת שבת ושבת הא זה דומה לוסת ומודה רב דראי' ט"ו שדינן לוסת קבוע א"כ גם גבי נגיחות שדינן שבת קמיית' לנגיחות ה' ו' ואייעד לכולא יומא וק' ותפשוט וד"ל דאף אם זה הראי' ט"ו שהיא למודה לראות בהם הי' ג' לראית' לוסת קבוע לא שדינן וברייתא דלמודה מיירי דראתה כבר ג"פ ורש"י לא חש וכתב רק דאנא קאמר' בתחילה ראי' וה"ה אם זה ראי' ט"ו היא פעם ג' מ"מ לא שדינן לראי' קמיית' ורש"י או או קאמר מלבד דזה דוחק כי לא מצינן במשנה רק כשתקבע ג"פ וק' הא לפעמים ל"ת עד שראתה ד"פ כנ"ל אף גם לכאורה מוכח דברייתא הכא דלמוד' ט"ו איירי דווקא עם הראי' שראה היום בט"ו קבעה ג"פ דאל"כ ק' לשמואל דס"ל דלעולם צריך ג"פ האי מתני' דתקשה לרב ק' ג"כ לשמואל דקתני היתה למודה לראות ט"ו ושינת' וק' טעמא דלמודה הא אינו למודה א"צ ג"פ וסגי בב"פ וקשי' לשמואל והלא זה סוגי' בכל הש"ס ויותר ק' להנך פוסקים כשמואל דצריך ג"פ כיון דתני כוותו שינת' לכ"א וכו' עיין בהרא"ש וק' הא אליבי' דרב נמי איירי בלמודה לראות בכ' א"כ גם כרב אתי' ואף די"ל כיון דסתם גמ' דחק' דייקא נמי דשבקינן וכו' זה דוחק ועיין בהה"מ פ"ח הנ"ל שכתב כיון דתני' כוותו וזה יוכל להיות גם כרב וביותר כיון דקתני דווקא למודה ובפרט הא הלכה כרב באיסור' וצ"ע) וע"ק האי למודה מאי למימרא אליבי' דשמואל הא בלא למוד' ג"כ צריך ג"פ לרב ניחא דאשמעינן דווקא למודה וא"ל דאשמעינן למודה כמו דמתרץ הגמ' על קו' דקארי לי' מ"ק לי' דה"א דעוקרת בתרתי הא זה מפורש במתני' דהכא דאין וסת נעקר עד שתקבענו וכו' ובאמת על סתם גמ' ג"כ ק' דמתרץ למודה אצטריך דה"א דעקרת' בב"פ הא זה מתני' מופרשת וא"ל דברייתא מפרש דברי המתני' הא זה כבר תנא לי' בברייתא שינתה וכו' וצ"ע. לכן י"ל דהכא איירי למודה דראתה מקדם ב"פ בט"ו והיות תשלש הוסת הקבוע ובחודש שלאחריו שינתה לט"ז וס"ל לרב ושמואל דשדינן זה הט"ו לוסת הקבוע וא"כ שפיר אשמעינן רבות' דלמוד' דה"א דשדינן זה הט"ו לוסת הדילג ולאחריו כאבעי' הגמ' בב"ק גבי נגיחות כיון דרואים דדילג עוד פעמים אשמועינן דשדינן ראי' ט"ו לוסת הקבוע וצריך עוד ג"פ בין לרב ובין לשמואל וז"ש רב למודה שאני כיון דבחודש הזה שראתה בו לט"ו נקבע וסת קבוע הוי למודה ואינו מהמנין ופריך הגמ' ודקארי לי' וכו' הא זה הוי לי' למודה ומשני ה"א דעקרת' בב"פ דה"א דאינו דומה למתני' כיון דאיכא ספק לא שדינן ראי' ט"ו לוסת החודש אלא לדילג קמ"ל וא"ש ולפ"ז דברי הרש"י בדיוק נאמר' אנא קאמרינן דוקא בהתחילה לראות ודברי הש"ך על נכון כי דבריו נאמר' בפירוש בגמ' ולק"מ אך עדיין יהי' קו' הנ"ל על הגמ' בב"ק במ"ע ותפשוט מהכא segments.en: Regarding the substance of the objection, however, it appears possible to defend the Shach. Indeed, my grandfather's challenge would otherwise be stronger against the Gemara in Bava Kamma itself, because the question there should be resolved from the sugya in Niddah, and the Shach's ruling appears explicit in the Gemara, as I will explain. Bava Kamma 34 asks: if an ox gored on Shabbos, Shabbos, Shabbos, then Sunday and Monday, do we assign the last Shabbos to the Shabbos pattern, making it forewarned for Shabbos but not weekdays, or to the two days following Shabbos, making it forewarned for all days? It also asks about an ox that gored on Thursday, Friday, Shabbos, Shabbos, etc., concerning the first Shabbos. At first glance this is difficult because the Gemara compares patterns of goring to the dispute of Rav and Shmuel regarding veset. Niddah 64 states: a woman was accustomed to seeing on the fifteenth and changed to the sixteenth, then the seventeenth, then the eighteenth; the prior dates are released and she is prohibited only from the eighteenth onward. The Gemara challenges Rav, and Rav answers, "one who was already accustomed is different." Rashi explains: since she was certainly accustomed to see on the fifteenth, we assign the fifteenth sightings to the preceding fifteenth sightings; Rav's rule applies only where she has just begun to see or to a woman with no veset. Accordingly, if a woman saw twice on the fifteenth and now sees a third time on the fifteenth, thereby completing a fixed veset, and then changes to the sixteenth and seventeenth, Rav agrees that she still needs another progression to the eighteenth, because the third fifteenth is assigned to the fixed veset. Rav's view that two progressions suffice applies only where she was beginning a new pattern, not where that very fifteenth sighting completed an established veset. If so, why does Bava Kamma remain uncertain concerning an ox that gored Thursday, Friday, Shabbos, then Shabbos and Shabbos? This seems exactly analogous: Rav agrees that the first Shabbos should be assigned to the Thursday-Friday-Shabbos sequence and the ox should become forewarned for all days. One might answer that even if the fifteenth sighting that she was accustomed to was the third sighting completing the fixed veset, we would not assign it there, and the Baraisa's case of an accustomed woman means that she had already seen three times previously; Rashi was not precise when he said only that Rav's rule applies at the beginning. But this is strained. We find in the Mishnah only that a veset is established after three sightings, and on this approach sometimes four would be required. Moreover, it appears that the Baraisa specifically means that with the current fifteenth sighting she completes the three sightings that establish the veset. Otherwise it would also be difficult according to Shmuel, who always requires three changes: the Baraisa says specifically that she was accustomed to the fifteenth and then changed; if she were not already accustomed, according to Shmuel she would still require three changes, so why emphasize that she was accustomed? This is a standard style of proof throughout the Talmud. It is especially difficult for the poskim who rule like Shmuel because the Baraisa's continuation, "she changed to the twenty-first," etc., supports him; see the Rosh. Yet that Baraisa could also fit Rav if it concerned someone already accustomed to the twentieth. One could say that because the anonymous Gemara strained to say "this is also precise," etc., this is still weak. See Maggid Mishneh in chapter 8, who writes that a Baraisa was taught in accordance with Shmuel, though it could fit Rav as well; and especially since it says specifically "accustomed," and the halacha usually follows Rav in prohibitory law, the matter requires study. There is another difficulty: what novelty does "accustomed" add according to Shmuel? Even without an established veset, three instances are required. According to Rav it is understandable, because the Baraisa teaches specifically that an established pattern is different. One cannot say that the novelty is that an established veset is uprooted only after three changes, for the Mishnah itself explicitly states that a veset is not uprooted until it is changed the requisite number of times. In truth, the Gemara's own answer that the case of an accustomed woman is needed because otherwise one might think it is uprooted after two occasions is difficult, since that too is explicit in the Mishnah. Nor can one say that the Baraisa merely explains the Mishnah, because it has already taught the sequence itself. Therefore it appears that the case is where she had previously seen twice on the fifteenth and with the present fifteenth sighting completes the fixed veset, and in the following month changes to the sixteenth. Rav and Shmuel both hold that this fifteenth belongs to the fixed veset. The Baraisa therefore teaches a novelty: one might have thought to assign that fifteenth to the new progressive pattern, as in the unresolved question in Bava Kamma, because the following sightings display a progression; it teaches instead that the fifteenth belongs to the fixed veset and another three changes are required according to both Rav and Shmuel. This is what Rav means by "one who was accustomed is different": since in that month the fifteenth sighting completed a fixed veset, she is already treated as accustomed and that sighting is not counted toward the new progression. The Gemara then asks why the original questioner did not recognize that this was an established pattern, and answers that one might have thought that because there is uncertainty whether to assign the fifteenth to the monthly veset or to the progressing veset, the established veset could be uprooted with two subsequent changes; the Baraisa teaches otherwise. Rashi's words are therefore exact: Rav's statement applies specifically when she begins to see, and Shach's ruling is correct because it is explicit in the Gemara. Still, the earlier difficulty returns against the unresolved question in Bava Kamma: why not resolve it from this? It appears to me that there is a distinction. Regarding a veset, we properly assign the fifteenth sighting to the preceding monthly veset rather than to the progressing veset, because there is no reason to displace a common monthly veset in favor of an uncommon progressing veset. Regarding an ox that gored on two weekdays, however, there remains reason to assign the Shabbos goring to the other Shabbos goreings, because there is an independent rationale that Shabbos is not part of the weekday pattern at all. The Mishnah speaks of an ox that is forewarned for Shabbos, and Rashi explains that on Shabbos the owner rests from work and the animal's disposition changes; the Yerushalmi explains that the animal sees clean white clothing. There is also a contrary consideration: it already gored twice on weekdays, but two occasions did not make it forewarned, and it subsequently passed through weekdays without goring, as Maharsha explains there. This reveals that it was not forewarned for weekdays but only for Shabbos, so the first Shabbos should not be assigned to the earlier weekdays. By contrast, in the veset case the fifteenth sighting is a full and ordinary sighting that can as naturally belong to the monthly veset as to the progressing veset. There is no reason to displace the common pattern. In addition, with a woman one must in any event wait some interval to observe the next sighting, so what difference is there whether she waits 30 or 31 days? Thus the goring case has an independent reason to separate Shabbos from the weekday sequence and is not truly parallel to veset in this respect. The difficulty therefore falls away, and the Shach's words are correct.

en_segments: Seif 5. Regarding what my grandfather, the Gaon of blessed memory, wrote in seif katan 4 on Shach, seif katan 26: the Shach concludes that if a woman saw on Rosh Chodesh of Shevat, Adar, and Nisan, and afterward skipped a month and saw in Sivan and then Av, we assign the Nisan sighting to the established monthly veset, so there are only two instances of an alternating-month veset. My grandfather challenged this from Bava Kamma, where the Gemara asks concerning an ox that gored on Thursday, Friday, Shabbos, Shabbos, and Shabbos: do we assign the first Shabbos to the first sequence, so that it became forewarned for all days, or to the later Shabbos sequence, so that it became forewarned only for Shabbos? The question remains unresolved, and Rambam in chapter 6 of Hilchos Nizkei Mamon likewise rules that it is doubtful. If so, the cases appear completely parallel. Since the question remains unresolved and a veset is a rabbinic matter, the doubt should be resolved leniently in every direction, assigning Nisan to the alternating veset rather than the monthly veset, so that she need be concerned only every second month. See there. Before addressing the substance, I wished to consider whether there is any practical difference between the Shach's stringent view and my grandfather's proof for leniency. In the case of a woman who saw in Shevat, Adar, Nisan, then Sivan and Av, the immediate uncertainty concerns Rosh Chodesh Elul. According to the Shach, since Nisan belongs to the fixed monthly veset, she is prohibited in Elul because that monthly veset has been skipped only twice. According to my grandfather, if we leniently assign Nisan to the alternating pattern, Rosh Chodesh Elul would be permitted. Beyond that, however, there initially seems to be no practical difference, because if she sees in Elul it becomes clear that she remained with the monthly veset. His entire basis for leniency was doubt; once she sees in Elul, the matter is clarified in favor of the earlier, more common monthly pattern. Thus the doubt would concern only Elul itself. Although I am young in years and wisdom and unfit to place my head between two great mountains, I cannot refrain from speaking. It appears that everyone should agree that she is prohibited in Elul. Even if we rule leniently that she established an alternating veset, as my grandfather says, I already cited in the preceding seif katan Rambam in chapter 8 of Hilchos Issurei Biah, who rules that even when she certainly establishes a progressively changing veset, she must nevertheless be concerned for the next month lest she establish a monthly veset. My grandfather himself earlier asked why the Mechaber omitted Rambam's view, which is also Tosafos's view. If, as explained there, Rambam deals even with a doubtful establishment of a changing veset and everyone agrees to that concern, then here too, where there are multiple doubts and the proposed leniency rests only on doubt, she certainly must be concerned. If Rambam deals with a fully established changing veset, all the more so here, where there are added doubts, everyone should agree with Rambam and Tosafos that she is prohibited on the coming Rosh Chodesh Elul. Thus it is clear that she is prohibited in Elul, and in Elul the doubt will be clarified. The difficulty against the Shach is then what practical difference it makes whether we assign Nisan to the established monthly veset. According to what I have said, Rosh Chodesh Elul is forbidden in any event, and when Elul arrives the doubt will be clarified. One cannot say that if Nisan is not assigned to the established monthly veset, the Shach holds it is also not assigned to the alternating veset, leaving her as a woman with no veset who requires examination before relations and concern for intervals and the like. That would be strained and excessively stringent: she certainly has either a monthly or alternating veset, and in such a doubt we certainly rule leniently. Moreover, according to the Shach in siman 184, even a woman without a fixed veset, within 30 days, is treated like a woman with a veset and does not require examination for her husband; by day 30 the doubt will have been clarified. Nor can one say that although Elul is forbidden because she might establish the monthly veset, she may have relations close to her expected veset and is prohibited only during the actual onah, whereas if the veset is already fixed she is prohibited even near it. Above in siman 184 it is explained that one must separate near the veset even after a single prior sighting. It would be very forced to distinguish that this applies only when the prior sighting cannot be attributed to another veset, whereas in a doubtful case we might assign it to the alternating veset and, although we remain concerned that it might belong to another pattern, not require separation near the veset because the entire matter is rabbinic and a doubt is lenient. One must therefore say, with difficulty, that according to the Shach, who definitely assigns Nisan to the fixed veset, once the time passes she may not have relations without expressly asking her, as explained above in siman 184, unlike the Rif and Rambam, who permit relations even if she is asleep. If the monthly veset is only a concern, however, everyone agrees with Rambam and Rif that after the time passes he may have relations with her even while she sleeps, because there is a double doubt: perhaps Nisan belongs to the alternating veset and it is not her time to see, and even if Nisan belongs to the monthly veset, perhaps she did not see. This may be my grandfather's intention. Still, with respect to the basic prohibition on Rosh Chodesh Elul there is no difference, for even my grandfather agrees she is forbidden then. It is impossible to ignore the possible alternating veset when Rambam and Tosafos are stringent even without such uncertainty. When Elul arrives, the doubt is clarified: if she sees, we see that she established the monthly veset; if she does not see, it is clear that she established the alternating veset. Thus the difference is whether her husband must ask her explicitly after the Elul onah, or may have relations without asking, according to Rif and Rambam. This would explain why Shach says simply that Nisan is assigned to the monthly veset and therefore she is prohibited, while my grandfather objects that the Gemara leaves the analogous question unresolved and a rabbinic doubt is lenient, so she need be concerned only every second month, meaning that after the Elul onah has passed her husband may have relations without explicitly asking. As to the prohibition on Rosh Chodesh Elul itself, my grandfather likewise agrees. There may, however, be a substantial practical difference concerning uprooting the veset. If she did not see on Rosh Chodesh Elul, she is certainly permitted afterward. Yet if she then sees on the twentieth of Tishrei and does not see on Rosh Chodesh Tishrei, according to the Shach she still has a fixed Rosh Chodesh veset, because she has not yet uprooted it three consecutive times. According to my grandfather, the monthly veset requires no uprooting at all, while the alternating veset that she established would require three occasions of uprooting. This too requires study, because it may be rejected.

segments.he: לח אא"כ היה בדוק לה. ואפי' עד בינוני שמבואר לעיל בסעיף ל"ו ג"כ מקרי בדוק לענין כתם אם יש בו כגריס ועוד ואינו בדוק היינו שאינו בדוק כלל רק שלקחתו מן השוק ונמצא בו שהוא בחזקת מלוכלך. ט"ז ודלא כב"ח:
segments.en: Seif katan 38: "unless it had been examined for her." Even an ordinary examination cloth described above in seif 36 is considered examined with respect to a stain larger than a gris. "Unexamined" means not examined at all, such as one taken from the marketplace and found in a state presumed to be soiled. Taz, unlike Bach.

segments.he: בדקה חלוקה. כן הוא לשון הטור והא דנקט בדקה ליכא למימר דמ"ה אצטריך לומר בדקה דאל"כ פשיטא שהיא טהורה אף בלא השאילתו לחברתה. דמ"מ קשה למה לי למתני בדקה אף אם לא בדקה מ"מ כיון שלקחתו מן השוק ושלא היה בחזקת מלוכלך ג"כ הוי כבדוק לענין כתם אם יש בו כגריס ועוד וכמ"ש לעיל ס"ק ל"ז (ואף דעת הב"ח כן הוא דודאי לא יחלוק על הטור והרשב"א שכתבו כן להדיא רק שדעתו דאף בחזקתו מלוכלך ממש מ"מ בקנוח ובדיקה טמאה מיותר כגריס ועוד אבל באמת זה אינו וכמ"ש הט"ז בס"ק כ"ט) וצ"ל דוקא נקט בדקתו להראות דדוקא כשבדקו פעם שנית כשפשטתו טהורה אבל לא בדקתו פעם ב' אע"פ שבדקתו כשלבשתו (פי' כ"ש כשלא בדקתו ממש אבל מ"מ היה בחזקת בדוק דאל"כ שתיהן טהורות וק"ל) שתיהן טמאות כל זה נ"ל פשוט שזה תמיהות הפרישה והב"ח על הטור וכוונת הב"ח בישוב דברי הטור כמ"ש ונסתלק בזה דברי הט"ז והש"ך מה שתירצו בזה ומתמיהים על הב"ח ולפי מה שכתבתי הכל נכון אכן דברי הב"ח בסעיף ל"ח צע"ק לפ"ז:
segments.en: "She examined her garment." This is the Tur's language. One cannot say that the word "examined" was needed because otherwise it would be obvious that she is pure even without having lent the garment to her friend. The difficulty remains: why say that she examined it? Even if she did not actually examine it, if she took it from the market when it was not presumed soiled, it likewise has the status of examined with respect to a stain larger than a gris, as I wrote above in seif katan 37. Bach certainly agrees with this, for he would not dispute the Tur and Rashba, who write it explicitly. Bach's view is only that even where the cloth is actually presumed soiled, nevertheless for wiping or examination she becomes impure with more than a gris; in truth that is incorrect, as Taz writes in seif katan 29. Rather, the Baraisa specifically says that she examined the garment to teach that only if she examined it a second time when she removed it is she pure. If she did not examine it a second time, even though she examined it when she put it on, or all the more so where she did not literally examine it but it was presumed clean, for otherwise both women would be pure, both women are impure. This appears to me straightforward. This is the basis of the Perishah's and Bach's question on the Tur, and this is Bach's intended resolution of the Tur, as I have explained. The answers of Taz and Shach, and their surprise at Bach, therefore fall away. According to this, however, Bach's words in seif 38 still require some study.

Even if she did not actually examine it, if she took it from the market when it was not presumed soiled, it likewise has the status of examined with respect to a stain larger than a gris, as I wrote above in seif katan 37. Bach certainly agrees with this, for he would not dispute the Tur and Rashba, who write it explicitly. Bach's view is only that even where the cloth is actually presumed soiled, nevertheless for wiping or examination she becomes impure with more than a gris; in truth that is incorrect, as Taz writes in seif katan 29. Rather, the Baraisa specifically says that she examined the garment to teach that only if she examined it a second time when she removed it is she pure. If she did not examine it a second time, even though she examined it when she put it on, or all the more so where she did not literally examine it but it was presumed clean, for otherwise both women would be pure, both women are impure. This appears to me straightforward. This is the basis of the Perishah's and Bach's question on the Tur, and this is Bach's intended resolution of the Tur, as I have explained. The answers of Taz and Shach, and their surprise at Bach, therefore fall away. According to this, however, Bach's words in seif 38 still require some study.

segments.he: האשה וכו' מה שקשה ע"ז מעד שאינו בדוק ע"ל סי' ק"צ ע"ש:
segments.en: The woman, etc. Regarding the difficulty from an examination cloth that was not checked, see above, siman 190; see there.

segments.he: וי"א דאין להתיר אלא ביושבת וכו' זהו דעת הטור והרא"ש דאף ר"י לא פליג אר"מ כי אם במזנקת דאיכא חדא לטיבות' אבל בשותת ועומדת דהוי תרתי לריעותא מודה ר"י דטמאה והקשה הב"ח א"כ מה פריך הגמ' השתא בחד ספקא מטהרין בב' ספיקא מבעי הא בב' ספיקא טהור אפי' בעומדת ושותתת ולק"מ דלכך לא הקשה הגמ' קושיא זו כי אם בתר דמסקינן דבב' ספיקא אף ר"מ מטהר ועכצ"ל דהך תרי ספיקא הוי יותר מחד צד לטיבות' דהא בחד צד לטיבות' מטמא ר"מ ובעי תרתי לטיבות' ומ"מ מטהר בב' ספיק' ש"מ הואיל ויש כאן ספק אולי לא בא מהאיש כלל נחשב כתרתי לטיבות' ומטהר ר"מ וא"כ מקש' הגמ' אח"כ שפיר השתא בחד ספק דיש כאן רק חדא לטיבותא מכשיר ר"י מכ"ש בב' ספיקות דע"כ הוי תרתי לטיבות' דהא ר"מ מטהר בי' פשיטא דמטהר ר"י ולק"מ ופשוט:
segments.en: "And some say that one may permit only when she is sitting," etc. This is the view of the Tur and the Rosh: even R' Yose disagrees with R' Meir only where the urine spurts, for then there is one favorable factor; but where it flows while she is standing, there are two adverse factors and R' Yose agrees that she is impure. Bach asks: if so, why does the Gemara ask, "If they purify with one doubt, all the more so with two doubts"? With two doubts she is pure even when standing and flowing. This is no difficulty. The Gemara asks this only after concluding that even R' Meir purifies in a case of two doubts. Necessarily, two doubts here are equivalent to more than one favorable factor, because R' Meir is stringent where there is only one favorable factor yet is lenient with two doubts. This shows that because there is also a doubt whether the blood came from the woman at all, the case is treated like two favorable factors, and even R' Meir is lenient. The Gemara can then properly ask that if R' Yose permits with only one doubt, where there is only one favorable factor, then all the more so he certainly permits with two doubts, which necessarily count as two favorable factors because even R' Meir permits there. The matter is straightforward.

segments.he: אבל אם נמצא בספל שאיש ואשה כו' טהורה בכל ענין וכתב הש"ך בסק"ו דהיינו בנמצא תוך הספל ואם נתכוין ליושבת דבריו מעיקרא ליתא דהא עומדת איכא חד לריעותא ומותר בס"ס ה"ה ביושבת ושותתת דהוי חד לריעותא ומותר בס"ס ואם נתכוין בעומד עכ"פ יהי' מקלחת דהוי חד לריעותא בזו אין דברי' מפורכ' אבל מ"מ אין לו ראי' ולשונו מורה דדייק ממשנה דקתני על המים וזהו אינו דהא אף ביושבת איירי ולכן אין לדבריו שורש:
segments.en: "But if it was found in a basin used by a man and a woman," etc., she is pure in every circumstance. Shach in seif katan 6 writes that this means where the blood was found inside the basin. If he means specifically where she was sitting, his words are unfounded, because when she stands there is one adverse factor and yet she is permitted through a double doubt; the same applies where she sits and the urine flows, which likewise has only one adverse factor and is permitted through a double doubt. If he means where she stood, then at least she must have urinated in a stream, which is one favorable factor. In that formulation his words are not refuted, but he still has no proof. His wording indicates that he inferred it from the Mishnah's phrase "upon the water," but that inference is incorrect, because the Mishnah also deals with a sitting woman. His position therefore has no basis.

segments.he: רק באשה שיש לה וסת עי' ש"ך שהאריך בסק"ז דלמה צריך דוקא וסת וקשה וכי לעולם לא תטמא לא שייך כיון דתטמא ברואה שלא בעת צרכי' ולכן מפרש דגם מהרי"ל מיירי באשה שלא ראתה וסת' כי אם ע"י מי רגלה ולכך הצריכה וסת עכ"ל אבל לבבי לא כן ידמה דא"כ דאשה זו אין רואה דם וסתה רק ע"י מי רגלי' וברור לפנינו דאשה זו רואה דם מקור במי רגלי' וא"כ איך התיר מהרי"ל בתשוב' אפי' באין לה וסת קבוע רק שדרכה תמיד מבלי להקדים ד"מ מכ' לכ' אף שלפעמים רואה כ"א או כ"ג וכדומה ע"ש וקשה הא וסת אין לה שנימא בי' חזקה אורח בזמנו בא וא"כ אם לאחר הפלג' י' ימים ראתה במי רגלי' מאין היתר לטהר' כיון שברור לן שרואה דם מהמקור תוך מי רגלים ולמה נטהר הראי' לאחר יו"ד להפלג' במי רגלים ונטמא הראי' לאחר כ' במי רגלים ודבר זה צע"ג לטהר אשה אשר ברור לן כי דם מן מקורה בא במי רגלי' כי אינה רואה כי אם בכה"ג ואין לה וסת קבוע רק הואיל ודרכ' מבלי להקדים אם פעם ופעמים הקדימ' יהי' טהורה ועוד מה כל חרדה שהחריד המהרי"ל באשה זו לטהרה כיון שאין דרכה לראות במי רגלה רק בזמן מוגבל ובזמן מוגבל אפי' בבדיקת מוך טמאה ואם בשביל שפעם א' שינת' במקר' ע"ז החריד כל חרדה והלא תמיד לא ראתה רק בזמן מוגבל ואם תמיד ראתה שלא בזמן מוגבל איך כ' מהרי"ל שרואה מכ' לכ' ואם הפשט דרואה מכ' לכ' בראי' פשוטה מה אריא מכ' לכ' הא בלא"ה כיון שראתה שלא במי רגלי' קושית הש"ך במקומו ולכן אמת יורה דרכו דמיירי דראתה מכ' לכ' כפשוט' ודברי הש"ך דאינו רואה רק במ"ר ליתא וכן מורין דברי מהרי"ל בתשוב' דלא כדבריו ובקושיא נראה דהא דכתב מהר"ל וכי לעולם לא תהא טמא' אין כונתו על עולמו של אשה דלא תהא טמאה כל ימי' דפשיטא תוכל להיות טמא ברואה שלא במי רגלי' כקושית הש"ך רק כונתו לעולם ברואה במי רגלי' תהי' ראי' זו לעולם טהור וזהו לא יתכן כיון דאין וסת לאשה זו עד שנאמר בה חזקה אורח בזמנו כו' רק רואה פעם בשעה זו ופעם בשעה זו וא"כ וכי לא ימלט שרוא' פ"א לאחר מי רגלי' דמאן מעכב הלא אין לה זמן מוגבל ואדרב' חימום מי רגלי' עלולין להביא דם כמ"ש מחברים וא"כ נטהר אשה והיא באמת ראתה דם גמור כי אין ספק ברב ימי ושנים שיזדמן שתהי' רואה פ"א וסתה רצוף למי רגלי'. וזהו כונתו ונכון ולכך אם יש לה עכ"פ זמן מוגבל לראי' מכ' לכ' אע"פ שאינו כוסת הקבוע מ"מ יצאנו קצת מידי ספק זה בתוך ימים אלו אמרינן דלא יזדמן שתראה דם מהמקור במי רגלי' דלא עלולה לראות בימים אלו אבל באין לה מוגבל מי יבחן אולי הראי' סמוך למי רגלי' וא"ש והמעיין במהרי"ל יראה שדברי נכונין וברורין עבק"א:
segments.en: "Only in a woman who has a veset." See Shach, who discusses at length in seif katan 7 why a fixed veset should be necessary. The argument "otherwise she would never become impure" does not apply, since she can become impure when she sees blood not in connection with urination. Shach therefore explains that Maharil too deals with a woman whose veset blood appears only when she urinates, and for that reason he required some form of veset. In my view this cannot be correct. If this woman never sees her veset blood except together with urine, then it is established before us that she does pass uterine blood together with urine. How then could Maharil permit even where she lacks a fixed veset and merely has an ordinary pattern not to see earlier than, for example, 20 days, although at times she sees on day 21 or 23, as is explicit in the responsum? Since she has no fixed veset regarding which we can invoke the presumption that her period comes at its time, if after only 10 days she sees blood with urine, on what basis can we declare it pure? We already know that her uterine blood can emerge with urine. Why should blood found with urine after 10 days be pure while blood found with urine after 20 days is impure? This is very difficult, particularly when one seeks to purify a woman concerning whom it is clear that blood from the source emerges with her urine, since according to this theory she sees only in that manner. She has no fixed veset, merely a habit not to see earlier than a certain time; if she once or twice sees earlier, shall she therefore be pure? Moreover, why did Maharil labor so greatly to permit this woman merely because she usually does not see with her urine except at a defined time, when at that defined time even an internal cloth examination would render her impure? If the concern is only that on one occasion she changed her pattern, why such extensive discussion when ordinarily she sees only at that defined time? If "she sees from 20 days to 20 days" meant an ordinary sighting unrelated to urination, then the Shach's original question has no force at all, because once she also sees at other times without urinating, she clearly can become impure. Therefore the plain truth is that Maharil means that she sees every 20 days in the ordinary sense, not only when urinating, and the responsum itself indicates this, unlike the Shach. The answer to the Shach's question is that Maharil's statement "otherwise she would never be impure" does not mean that she would remain pure throughout her entire life, for obviously she could become impure if she saw blood not while urinating. Rather, his meaning is that whenever blood appears with urination, that type of sighting would always be declared pure. That cannot be correct for a woman who has no fixed or even bounded time of seeing, who at times sees now and at times later. Over many days and years it is inevitable that on some occasion her real uterine flow will happen to coincide with urination. Indeed, the warmth of urination can itself precipitate blood, as the authorities write. If we always purify her in such a circumstance, we will sometimes purify a woman who actually saw ordinary uterine blood. This is Maharil's concern. If, however, she has at least a bounded pattern, such as not seeing before 20 days, then within those earlier days we have partially escaped this concern: we may say that it is unlikely that uterine blood happened to emerge with the urine when she is not prone to see during that period. When there is no such boundary, who can determine whether the sighting adjacent to urination was her actual veset? This is the correct explanation, and one who studies Maharil will see that these words are clear and correct. See Birkei Yosef.

segments.he: ואם מצאה דם תוך מי רגלי' וגם על העד כו' י"א דהיא טמאה וכו' הש"ך בס"ק ח' כתב דהוא ללא צורך כיון דכבר פסק לעיל להחמיר זולת במקלחת ע"ש ומלבד דיש לדחות דבשלמא לעיל אמרינן אי איתא דממי רגלי' באה למה נמצא על שפת ולא תוך הספל משא"כ בבדיקה די"ל שיורי טיפת דם ממי רגלים נשארין דבוקין בצדדין בפרוזדר ובבדיקת עד נמצאו ואין כאן ריעות' כלל אף גם נראה דדעת הלזה אם נמצא ע"ג העד אין תולין כלל במי רגלי' דאין תולין במי רגלי' רק ברואה אבל בנמצא על העד אין ענין כלל למי רגלי' וא"כ בבדקה בעד בלתי בדוק הרי זה נימא כמו לעיל בסי' ק"צ ע"ש משא"כ אלו הוי אמרינן דהיינו ראתה במי רגלי' ראתה ע"ג עד רק אסורה כמו בנמצאת על שפת הספל כמ"ש הש"ך א"כ טומאה זו מכח ספק דלמא הדרי מ"ר למקור כנ"ל ובעד שאינו בדוק הרי כאן ס"ס דלמא מעלמא ואת"ל מבדיקה דלמא מן מי רגלי' ולזה קמ"ל דגבי בדיקה לא תלינן כלל במי רגלים וא"כ חזר הדין לדלעיל בסי' ק"ץ דאפי' עד שאינו בדוק טמא וא"ש:
segments.en: "And if she found blood within the urine and also upon the examination cloth," etc., some say that she is impure. Shach in seif katan 8 writes that this is unnecessary, because above we already ruled stringently except where she urinates in a stream. Besides the fact that one can answer that above we say: if the blood came from the urine, why was it found on the rim and not inside the basin, whereas with an examination it is quite possible that remnants of a drop of blood from the urine remained attached to the sides of the vaginal passage and were then found on the cloth, so there is no adverse factor at all, it also appears that according to this opinion, when blood is found on the cloth we do not attribute it to urine at all. Attribution to urine applies only to blood seen while urinating; blood found on an examination cloth has no inherent connection to urination. Therefore, if she examined with a cloth that had not been checked, this is governed by the law explained above in siman 190. If instead we said that this is simply a case where she saw blood with urine and also on the cloth, and she is forbidden only as in the case where blood is found on the rim of the basin, as Shach explains, then her impurity would be only because of the doubt that the urine may have returned to the source. With an unchecked cloth there would then be a double doubt: perhaps the blood came from elsewhere, and even if it came from the examination, perhaps it came from the urine. The ruling therefore teaches that in the context of an examination we do not attribute the blood to urine at all, and the case reverts to the law above in siman 190, where even an unchecked cloth can render her impure. This is proper.

segments.he: רק קרטין קרטין כמו חול וכו' עי' ט"ז סק"ד שהאריך וסוף דבריו דאפי' בנמצא חצף אדמה וקרטין שלא בשעת הטלת מי רגלים א"כ שייך הדין הנאמר ברמ"א והגאון חכם צבי בתשובתיו השיגו דלא מיירי הר"ן והרמ"א רק אחר מי רגלי' אבל זולתו לא והגאון שב יעקב עמד לימין הט"ז דמידי טעמא דר"ן דלא שכיחי לראות בקרטין וא"כ אף שלא בשעת מי רגלי' נמי לא שכיח ודברים אלו ליתא דהא איירי ע"כ בשנמחו כמ"ש הב"ה וד"מ וכ"כ הש"ך סקי"א ע"ש וא"כ קשיא לי הך סוגיא דגמ' דהמפלת כמין יבחושי' ושעורין דאמרו חכמים תטיל למי' אם נמחו טמאה וכי דרכה של אשה לראות כמין יבחושין וכדומה ומ"ש יבחושין ומ"ש קרטין (א) והר"ן מיירי אפי' אינה מרגשת כאב כמ"ש הט"ז בעצמו אלא ברור חלילה לנו להתיר דאם נמוחו דם גמורה הן רק במי רגלי' בלא"ה יש כאן היתר דהא רואה במי רגלי' ור"י מטהר לגמרי אפי' בכל צדדין ריעות' רק ר"מ מטמא כמ"ש הר"ן דחייש למעוטי דלמא הדר מי רגלי' למקור ואייתי ס"ל להר"ן אייתי דם אמרינן אבל קרטין לא אמרינן כי יותר שכיח לתלות קרטין במי רגלי' שהיא תולדת כליות ומשם מתמצי המי רגלי' ובאין כנודע משנתלות במקור דאין שכיח להוליד קרטין (ב) אבל בראי' שלא במי רגלי' דאין סברא לתלותן במי רגלים כלל וכל בדיקות מסתמא הן במקור מהיכי תיתי לתלותן במי רגלים ומה טיבו של מי רגלי' לכאן ואנו תולין במקור וכיון שנמחו דם שנימוח טמא וביחוד בעובדא דט"ז דהרגישה כאב למעל' ממקור וא"כ מה טיבו של כליות לכאן שהן באחורי' בצד סיום השדרה ויותר ברור דם מהמקור קאתי והג' שב יעקב ביקש לומר דיש חילוק בין קרטין להך דראתה כדמות חול דזהו אינו מחמת מכה שבכליות ומה ישיב על הך דאשה שהפילה כמין קליפות והעידו רופאין שאשה מכה יש לה במעים ומ"מ אם נמוחו טמאה ועיין מש"ל סי' קפ"ח ותמהני מחכם הנ"ל שבסבר' דקות שאין להן שורש בש"ס ופוסקים קודמים ובסבר' מי יאמר ואפשר דשאני זה מהך דחול ביקש להתיר איסור חמור כזה ובפרט בבדיק' שהיא איסור של תורה ואלו אמר להחמיר לא הינו שומעין בסברות דקות כזה ופשיטא להקל ובמחילה מכבודו הרמה שכתב על הגאון חכם צבי שדבריו הן דבר שפתי' שפת יתר ולא נאות לכתוב כן כי דבריו בזה המה ברורין וח"ו להתיר בקרטין בלי מי רגלי' ואם לסמוך על רופאין הלא אין ענין זה לכאן ועמש"ל סי' קפ"ח אבל זולת זה ח"ו להתיר קרטין כמש"ל דמ"ש קרטין ומ"ש קליפות וכדומה ולכן אין להתיר כנ"ל:
segments.en: "Only small granules like sand," etc. See Taz, seif katan 4, who discusses this at length and concludes that even if earth-like particles and granules are found not at the time of urination, the Rama's ruling applies. Chacham Tzvi objected in his responsa that Ran and Rama deal only with particles found after urination, not otherwise. Shevut Yaakov defended Taz, reasoning that Ran's point is that women do not ordinarily discharge blood in the form of granules, so this remains uncommon even when not associated with urination. These words are incorrect. The case necessarily concerns granules that dissolve, as Beit Yosef and Darkei Moshe write, and as Shach states in seif katan 11. If so, the Gemara's discussion of a woman who miscarries things resembling gnats or barley grains is difficult: the Sages say that she should place them in water, and if they dissolve she is impure. Does a woman ordinarily see blood in the form of gnats and the like? What difference is there between gnats and granules? Ran deals even where she feels no pain, as Taz himself writes. Rather, heaven forbid that we permit when the particles dissolve, for then they are actual blood. The point is only that where they appear with urine there is an independent ground for leniency: R' Yose purifies entirely even with all the adverse factors, while R' Meir is stringent because he is concerned for a minority case that perhaps the urine returned to the source and brought blood with it. Ran holds that one may say this regarding blood, but not regarding granules, because it is more plausible to attribute granules to the urinary tract, which derives from the kidneys and through which urine is filtered and passes, than to the uterus, where formation of granules is uncommon. But where the particles are seen not with urine and there is no reason at all to attribute them to the urinary tract, and ordinary internal examinations are presumed to reach the uterine source, why should one connect them to urine? We attribute them to the source; if they dissolve, they are dissolved blood and she is impure. This is especially true in the Taz's case, where she felt pain above the uterine area. What connection do the kidneys have there, when they lie toward the back near the end of the spine? It is much clearer that the blood came from the source. Shevut Yaakov sought to distinguish between granules and the case where she sees matter like sand, saying that the latter results from an injury in the kidneys. What then will he answer concerning a woman who discharged something like peels, where physicians testified that she had an intestinal wound, yet if the matter dissolved she was impure? See what I wrote above in siman 188. I am astonished that this eminent authority relied upon fine distinctions without roots in the Talmud or earlier poskim to permit such a severe prohibition, especially in the case of an internal examination, which can involve a Torah prohibition. Had he used such subtle reasoning to be stringent we would not necessarily accept it, all the more so to be lenient. With due respect, his criticism of Chacham Tzvi as mere excess language was inappropriate, for Chacham Tzvi's words here are clear. Heaven forbid permitting granules when there was no urination. Reliance upon physicians is a different issue, as explained above in siman 188; absent that, granules must not be permitted, as explained, for there is no relevant difference between granules, peels, and similar matter.

en_segments: The woman, etc. Regarding the difficulty from an examination cloth that was not checked, see above, siman 190; see there.

"And some say that one may permit only when she is sitting," etc. This is the view of the Tur and the Rosh: even R' Yose disagrees with R' Meir only where the urine spurts, for then there is one favorable factor; but where it flows while she is standing, there are two adverse factors and R' Yose agrees that she is impure. Bach asks: if so, why does the Gemara ask, "If they purify with one doubt, all the more so with two doubts"? With two doubts she is pure even when standing and flowing. This is no difficulty. The Gemara asks this only after concluding that even R' Meir purifies in a case of two doubts. Necessarily, two doubts here are equivalent to more than one favorable factor, because R' Meir is stringent where there is only one favorable factor yet is lenient with two doubts. This shows that because there is also a doubt whether the blood came from the woman at all, the case is treated like two favorable factors, and even R' Meir is lenient. The Gemara can then properly ask that if R' Yose permits with only one doubt, where there is only one favorable factor, then all the more so he certainly permits with two doubts, which necessarily count as two favorable factors because even R' Meir permits there. The matter is straightforward.

"But if it was found in a basin used by a man and a woman," etc., she is pure in every circumstance. Shach in seif katan 6 writes that this means where the blood was found inside the basin. If he means specifically where she was sitting, his words are unfounded, because when she stands there is one adverse factor and yet she is permitted through a double doubt; the same applies where she sits and the urine flows, which likewise has only one adverse factor and is permitted through a double doubt. If he means where she stood, then at least she must have urinated in a stream, which is one favorable factor. In that formulation his words are not refuted, but he still has no proof. His wording indicates that he inferred it from the Mishnah's phrase "upon the water," but that inference is incorrect, because the Mishnah also deals with a sitting woman. His position therefore has no basis.

"Only in a woman who has a veset." See Shach, who discusses at length in seif katan 7 why a fixed veset should be necessary. The argument "otherwise she would never become impure" does not apply, since she can become impure when she sees blood not in connection with urination. Shach therefore explains that Maharil too deals with a woman whose veset blood appears only when she urinates, and for that reason he required some form of veset. In my view this cannot be correct. If this woman never sees her veset blood except together with urine, then it is established before us that she does pass uterine blood together with urine. How then could Maharil permit even where she lacks a fixed veset and merely has an ordinary pattern not to see earlier than, for example, 20 days, although at times she sees on day 21 or 23, as is explicit in the responsum? Since she has no fixed veset regarding which we can invoke the presumption that her period comes at its time, if after only 10 days she sees blood with urine, on what basis can we declare it pure? We already know that her uterine blood can emerge with urine. Why should blood found with urine after 10 days be pure while blood found with urine after 20 days is impure? This is very difficult, particularly when one seeks to purify a woman concerning whom it is clear that blood from the source emerges with her urine, since according to this theory she sees only in that manner. She has no fixed veset, merely a habit not to see earlier than a certain time; if she once or twice sees earlier, shall she therefore be pure? Moreover, why did Maharil labor so greatly to permit this woman merely because she usually does not see with her urine except at a defined time, when at that defined time even an internal cloth examination would render her impure? If the concern is only that on one occasion she changed her pattern, why such extensive discussion when ordinarily she sees only at that defined time? If "she sees from 20 days to 20 days" meant an ordinary sighting unrelated to urination, then the Shach's original question has no force at all, because once she also sees at other times without urinating, she clearly can become impure. Therefore the plain truth is that Maharil means that she sees every 20 days in the ordinary sense, not only when urinating, and the responsum itself indicates this, unlike the Shach. The answer to the Shach's question is that Maharil's statement "otherwise she would never be impure" does not mean that she would remain pure throughout her entire life, for obviously she could become impure if she saw blood not while urinating. Rather, his meaning is that whenever blood appears with urination, that type of sighting would always be declared pure. That cannot be correct for a woman who has no fixed or even bounded time of seeing, who at times sees now and at times later. Over many days and years it is inevitable that on some occasion her real uterine flow will happen to coincide with urination. Indeed, the warmth of urination can itself precipitate blood, as the authorities write. If we always purify her in such a circumstance, we will sometimes purify a woman who actually saw ordinary uterine blood. This is Maharil's concern. If, however, she has at least a bounded pattern, such as not seeing before 20 days, then within those earlier days we have partially escaped this concern: we may say that it is unlikely that uterine blood happened to emerge with the urine when she is not prone to see during that period. When there is no such boundary, who can determine whether the sighting adjacent to urination was her actual veset? This is the correct explanation, and one who studies Maharil will see that these words are clear and correct. See Birkei Yosef.

"And if she found blood within the urine and also upon the examination cloth," etc., some say that she is impure. Shach in seif katan 8 writes that this is unnecessary, because above we already ruled stringently except where she urinates in a stream. Besides the fact that one can answer that above we say: if the blood came from the urine, why was it found on the rim and not inside the basin, whereas with an examination it is quite possible that remnants of a drop of blood from the urine remained attached to the sides of the vaginal passage and were then found on the cloth, so there is no adverse factor at all, it also appears that according to this opinion, when blood is found on the cloth we do not attribute it to urine at all. Attribution to urine applies only to blood seen while urinating; blood found on an examination cloth has no inherent connection to urination. Therefore, if she examined with a cloth that had not been checked, this is governed by the law explained above in siman 190. If instead we said that this is simply a case where she saw blood with urine and also on the cloth, and she is forbidden only as in the case where blood is found on the rim of the basin, as Shach explains, then her impurity would be only because of the doubt that the urine may have returned to the source. With an unchecked cloth there would then be a double doubt: perhaps the blood came from elsewhere, and even if it came from the examination, perhaps it came from the urine. The ruling therefore teaches that in the context of an examination we do not attribute the blood to urine at all, and the case reverts to the law above in siman 190, where even an unchecked cloth can render her impure. This is proper.

"Only small granules like sand," etc. See Taz, seif katan 4, who discusses this at length and concludes that even if earth-like particles and granules are found not at the time of urination, the Rama's ruling applies. Chacham Tzvi objected in his responsa that Ran and Rama deal only with particles found after urination, not otherwise. Shevut Yaakov defended Taz, reasoning that Ran's point is that women do not ordinarily discharge blood in the form of granules, so this remains uncommon even when not associated with urination. These words are incorrect. The case necessarily concerns granules that dissolve, as Beit Yosef and Darkei Moshe write, and as Shach states in seif katan 11. If so, the Gemara's discussion of a woman who miscarries things resembling gnats or barley grains is difficult: the Sages say that she should place them in water, and if they dissolve she is impure. Does a woman ordinarily see blood in the form of gnats and the like? What difference is there between gnats and granules? Ran deals even where she feels no pain, as Taz himself writes. Rather, heaven forbid that we permit when the particles dissolve, for then they are actual blood. The point is only that where they appear with urine there is an independent ground for leniency: R' Yose purifies entirely even with all the adverse factors, while R' Meir is stringent because he is concerned for a minority case that perhaps the urine returned to the source and brought blood with it. Ran holds that one may say this regarding blood, but not regarding granules, because it is more plausible to attribute granules to the urinary tract, which derives from the kidneys and through which urine is filtered and passes, than to the uterus, where formation of granules is uncommon. segments.he: חוששת לולד. ומטמאינן לה טומאת נקבה מספק:
segments.en: She must be concerned that it was a child. We therefore impose upon her, out of doubt, the impurity period of one who gave birth to a female.

segments.he: לא עלתה לה טבילה. אלא צריכה ז' נקיים אחר י"ד יום כדלעיל ס"א ומשמע דבמפלת ליכא מאן דמחמיר להצריכה פ"א יום וסגי לה בז' נקיי' אחר י"ד יום וכ"נ מדברי האחרונים ומ"מ נראה דבעל נפש יחמיר לפרוש ממנה ליל מ"א וליל פ"א משום ספק זכר או נקבה:
segments.en: Her immersion did not count. Rather, she requires seven clean days after the 14 days, as above in seif 1. It appears that in the case of a miscarriage no authority requires her to wait 81 days; seven clean days after 14 days suffice, and this also appears from the later authorities. Nevertheless, it seems that a scrupulous person should separate from her on the night of day 41 and the night of day 81 because of the doubt whether the fetus was male or female.

segments.he: וה"מ כו'. נ"ט א' וער"נ ד"ה תרומה כו':
segments.en: This applies only, etc. See Ran, s.v. "terumah," regarding the first reason.

segments.he: וכן אם כו'. ערא"ש דפ"ג ס"ב ועוד כתב דלא מזדקקי רבנן לשבועות כו' וכן היה מחמיר כו' ואף שאינו מצד הדין כמ"ש הרא"ש שם וכל אלו חומרות כו' וכ"כ המרדכי מ"מ כתב שיש להחמיר כמ"ש ס"פ המדיר זיל חזי אי איתשיל כו'. וכמ"ש נשבע להרע ולא ימיר ובפרק השולח (ל"ד ל"ה) נמנעו להשביעה וכיוצא:
segments.en: Likewise if, etc. See Rosh, chapter 3, siman 2. He further writes that the Sages did not ordinarily attend to oaths, etc., and that he himself would act stringently, etc. Although this is not required by strict law, as the Rosh writes there, "all these are stringencies," and Mordechai writes likewise, nevertheless he states that one should be stringent. This is like what is stated at the end of chapter HaMadir: "Go see whether she sought release," etc.; and like the verse, "He swears to his own hurt and does not change," and chapter HaSholeach, 34-35, where they refrained from administering an oath, and similar cases.

segments.he: כאימרא. כשה של קרבן כדירים דיר של קרבן כירושלים דחומות העיר ומגדליה משירי הלשכה אתו. הרא"ש. והר"ן פי' כירושלים כקרבנות שבירושלים:
segments.en: "Like an imra." Meaning like the lamb of a korban. "Like pens" means the pen of sacrificial animals. "Like Jerusalem" refers, according to the Rosh, to the city's walls and towers, which came from the surplus of the chamber. Ran explains "like Jerusalem" to mean like the korbanos offered in Jerusalem.

segments.he: אם נדר בשלהן כו'. דברי הרב אינם מכוונים והעולה מהגהת מרדכי הוא דאם אמר ככר זה עלי כשלחן שבמקדש או כאחד מכלי הקודש הוי נדר דהתפיס בדבר הנדור אבל אם נדר או נשבע בשלחן הקדש או בא' מכלי הקדש אינו כלום (כדלקמן סימן רל"ז ס"ו) אבל המתפיס או נודר בשלחן סתם ואין רצונו כשלחן שבמקדש שיצטרך התרה בע"ה אין לנו ובנדרים הלך אחר לשון בני אדם כדלקמן סי' רי"ז ואולי משמע ליה להרב מדמסיים בהגהת מרדכי דבע"ה צריך התרה כדאיתא בפ"ב דנדרים גבי נדר בחרם כו' (כדלקמן סימן ר"ח סעיף ב') ולא מדמי ליה לנדר בתורה (לקמן סימן רי"ג) דמייתי שם ראייה דאין צריך התרה וקי"ל דבע"ה צריך התרה אלמא דבא לדמותו לגמרי לנדר () [צ"ל בחרם] בתורה דיש במשמעותו ב' לשונות וצריך התרה בע"ה ה"ה הכא ודוחק וצ"ע:
segments.en: "If he vowed by theirs," etc. The Rama's words are not precise. The conclusion of Hagahos Mordechai is that if he says, "This loaf is forbidden to me like the table in the Mikdash," or like one of the sacred vessels, it is a valid vow because he associated the permitted object with something whose sanctity resulted from a vow. But if he vows or swears "by the sacred table" or "by one of the sacred vessels," it is nothing, as below in siman 237, seif 6. If one associates his vow with an ordinary table, or simply vows "by the table" without intending the table of the Mikdash, a layman should not require release, because with vows we follow ordinary human language, as below in siman 217. Perhaps the Rama inferred from the conclusion of Hagahos Mordechai, which says that a layman requires release, as stated in chapter 2 of Nedarim concerning one who vows by cherem, see below siman 208, seif 2, and does not compare it to one who vows by the Torah, below siman 213, which Hagahos Mordechai cites there as proof that release is unnecessary. Since we rule that a layman does require release in the former case, perhaps the Rama understood that the table case is entirely analogous to a vow by cherem or by the Torah, expressions that can bear two meanings, and therefore a layman requires release here as well. This is strained and requires study.

segments.he: מותרים. לפי שכל אלו אסורין מצד עצמן וא"כ אי אפשר לומר על דבר היתר שיהיה כזה דהא א"א שיהא גם זה אסור מצד עצמו כזה. ט"ז: (וזה הכלל כל שמשים דברים המותרים כדברים האסורים אם אותו דבר איסור יכול לעשותה בנדר הרי אלו אסורים ואם אינו יכול לעשותה בנדר הרי אלו מותרים. הרמב"ם) :
segments.en: They are permitted. All these items are forbidden intrinsically. It is therefore impossible to say that a permitted object should become "like this," because the permitted object cannot itself become intrinsically forbidden in the same manner. Taz. Rambam gives this rule: whenever one compares permitted objects to prohibited objects, if the prohibited object could itself have been created through a vow, the permitted object becomes forbidden; if it could not have been made prohibited through a vow, the permitted objects remain permitted.

segments.he: פתח. כתב הר"ן דאין פותחין לו בכבוד אמו כלומר אלו היה יודע שלא יהא כבוד לאמו בכך לא היה נודר דל"ת כיון דליתא אלא מדרבנן פותחין בכך קמ"ל וכתב ב"י בשם תשובת הרשב"ץ על מי שנאנס לאסור אשה א' והתפיסה בדבר האסור י"ל דבמקום אונס לא אחמרו רבנן להצריכו שאלה:
segments.en: "An opening." Ran writes that we do not open for him on the basis of his mother's honor, by saying, "Had you known that this would dishonor your mother, would you have vowed?" One might have thought that because the prohibition is only rabbinic, such an opening could be used, so he teaches otherwise. Beit Yosef cites a responsum of Rashbatz concerning one who was compelled to prohibit a certain woman to himself and associated the vow with an intrinsically prohibited object: it is possible that in a case of duress the Sages did not impose the stringency of requiring release.

segments.he: בשאר. והב"ח פוסק דהשתא כ"ע כע"ה הן אפילו בשאר נדרים ודברי הר"ב נראין עיקר. ש"ך:
segments.en: "Regarding other vows." Bach rules that nowadays everyone is treated as a layman even regarding other vows. The Rama's words appear primary. Shach.

segments.he: אחד כו'. מתני' רפ"ד דנזיר וגמ' דשבועות כ"ט ב':
segments.en: One, etc. Mishnah at the beginning of chapter 4 of Nazir and Gemara, Shevuos 29b.

segments.he: או דבר כו' כעניית כו'. כמש"ש ל"ו א' בו קבלת דברים ומזה הטעם כמוציא מפיו דמי בתוספתא פ"ג דנזיר האומר לחבירו הריני נזיר ואת אם אמר הן שניהן אסורין ואם לאו הוא אסור וחבירו מותר כו' ע"ש: אבל כו'. עש"ך וברפ"ה דנדרים מ"ו הא מינס וכו' ובפ"ז דכתובות (ע' א') המדיר את אשתו כו' ואי צריך לקבלתה לא פריך וכיון דמשועבד לה כו' וכן בנדרים רפ"ב (ט"ו ב') ועוד דא"כ היא נתנה אצבע כו':
segments.en: Or an expression, etc., such as answering, etc. As stated there, 36a, that an affirmative response constitutes acceptance of the matter. For this reason it is treated as though he himself uttered it. Tosefta, chapter 3 of Nazir: if one says to his fellow, "I am a nazir, and you?" and the fellow says yes, both are forbidden; if he says no, only the first is forbidden and his fellow is permitted. See there. "But," etc. See Shach, and the beginning of chapter 5 of Nedarim 46a, "is he then forbidden," etc.; and chapter 7 of Kesubos 70a concerning one who vows to deprive his wife, etc. If her acceptance were required, the Gemara could not ask there, since he is obligated to support her, etc. Likewise at the beginning of chapter 2 of Nedarim 15b; moreover, if so, she herself caused the prohibition, etc.

segments.he: תוך כ"ד. היינו שלום עליך רבי. פרישה:
segments.en: Within toch k'dei dibbur, namely the time required to say, "Shalom alecha, rebbi." Perishah.

segments.he: תוך כ"ד לנדרו. אבל לא תוך כ"ד למחאתן ולא אמרינן מאחר שחזר תוך כדי דבור למחאתן והם מיחו בו תוך כ"ד לנדרו דזה יחשב תכ"ד וכה"ג אמרינן בפרק שבועות העדות לענין חזרה וכפירת עדים שכאן אין האחרים שייכים לנדרו שתהא מחאה שלהם סומכת נדרו לחזרה כמ"ש הראב"ד ודלא כב"י שלא ידע כוונתו ונראה דגם הרמב"ם והטור מודים לזה כ"כ בד"מ ומביאו הדרישה וכ"כ הב"ח וכן מסיק בכסף משנה גופיה סוף פ"ב מהל' שבועות:
segments.en: Within toch k'dei dibbur of his vow, but not merely within toch k'dei dibbur of their protest. We do not say that because he retracted within toch k'dei dibbur of their protest, and they protested within toch k'dei dibbur of his vow, the entire sequence is considered one toch k'dei dibbur, even though a similar rule is stated in chapter Shevuas HaEdus regarding retraction and the denial of witnesses. Here the others have no legal participation in his vow that would connect their protest to his vow and thereby connect his retraction, as Ra'avad writes. This is unlike Beit Yosef, who did not understand his intention. It appears that Rambam and Tur likewise agree to this. Darkei Moshe writes this, and Derishah cites it; Bach writes likewise, and Kesef Mishneh himself concludes so at the end of chapter 2 of Hilchos Shevuos.

en_segments: Within toch k'dei dibbur, namely the time required to say, "Shalom alecha, rebbi." Perishah.

segments.he: כלום. לפי שדעתו אגוילין ואינן כלום:
segments.en: It is nothing, because his intent is upon the parchment sheets, which have no sanctity by themselves.

segments.he: עם הארץ. וכבר נתבאר לעיל סי' ר"ה דבזה"ז לכ"ע כע"ה דיינינן להו. ש"ך:
segments.en: A layman. It has already been explained above in siman 205 that nowadays, according to all opinions, we treat people as laymen. Shach.

segments.he: שכתוב. הראב"ד והר"ן כתבו הטעם מפני שיש בה קרבנות ואזכרות שהן כדבר הנדור שע"י הכתיבה והכנה לקדושה הן קדושות ולפ"ז כ"ש אם אמר בפי' אני נודר באזכרות שבה דהוי נדר אע"פ שאין כוונתו על איסור ונדר הכתוב בה וכן אם נדר במקצת יריעות שבתורה אע"פ שאין כתוב באותן יריעות איסור או נדר כיון שיש בהן אזכרות או קרבנות הוי נדר וכ' הט"ז ונ"ל דמי שנתחייב שבועה לא יתנו לו שבועה בלשון זה הריני נשבע בספר תורה דאפשר דאתי להורות לו היתר ויאמר דדעתיה אגוילים אא"כ שמניח ידו עליה דאז דינו כמו שאוחזה בידו:
segments.en: "That is written." Ra'avad and Ran explain that the reason is that the Torah contains korbanos and Divine Names, which are like matters whose sanctity comes through designation, since by writing and preparation for holiness they become sacred. According to this, all the more so if he says explicitly, "I vow by the Divine Names contained in it," the vow takes effect even though he does not intend the prohibitions and vows written in the Torah. Likewise, if he vows by some of the Torah's parchment sheets, even if those sheets contain no prohibition or vow, since they contain Divine Names or passages concerning korbanos it is a vow. Taz writes: it appears to me that when one is obligated to take an oath, they should not administer it with the formula, "I hereby swear by the Sefer Torah," because he might later rationalize that his intention was only to the parchment. Rather, he should place his hand upon it; then the law is as though he holds it in his hand.

en_segments: It is nothing, because his intent is upon the parchment sheets, which have no sanctity by themselves.

segments.he: מותר כו'. נראה דהיינו מסתמא אבל אם היה הטעם יין או בשר קשה לו וכה"ג אזלינן בתר כוונתו כדלקמן סי' רי"ח ואסור בטעמן:
segments.en: It is permitted, etc. It appears that this is the ordinary presumption. But if the reason he vowed was that wine or meat is difficult for him, or the like, we follow his intent, as below in siman 218, and he is forbidden even in their taste.

segments.he: אסור בתבשיל שיש בו טעם יין. ע"ל סי' צ"ח ס"ק ה' כתבתי דיש לסמוך אטעימת ישראל דהתירה אף בזמן הזה והלכך אם יש אחר שרשאי לטעום יכול לסמוך עליו ואם אין כאן אחר משערין בס' מיהו כל זה שלא במינו אבל במינו אפילו באלף לא בטיל כדבסעיף שאח"ז וע"ל סימן ק"ב:
segments.en: He is forbidden in a cooked food that contains the taste of wine. See above, siman 98, seif katan 5, where I wrote that one may rely upon tasting by a Jew where such tasting is permitted even nowadays. Therefore, if another person is present who may taste it, he can rely on that person's assessment. If no one else is available, we measure against 60. All this applies when the forbidden flavor is a different type from the food; with the same type, however, even one part in 1,000 is not nullified in the context of a vow, as in the following seif. See also siman 102.

segments.he: מי כו'. למד מסעיף שקדם:
segments.en: One who, etc. This is learned from the preceding seif.

segments.he: וכ"ש קהל כו'. ועש"ך בשם רש"ל שחולק על זה מגמ' פ"ק דחולין (י"ז א') וכדברי הרא"ש בתירוץ בתרא:
segments.en: All the more so a community, etc. See Shach in the name of Maharshal, who disagrees based on the Gemara in the first chapter of Chullin, 17a, and in accordance with the Rosh's latter answer.

segments.he: מותר כו'. ר"ל אבל לאכול ולשתות אסור וכמ"ש בתוספתא פ"ד מותר ליכנס לביתו ולרחוץ עמו בצונן ואסור לאכול ולשתות וט"ס וצ"ל ולשתות עמו בצונן דלא כהרא"ש וטור שמתירין גם לאכול ולשתות כיון שאין פיו ולבו שוין כמ"ש בפ"ג דתרומות:
segments.en: It is permitted, etc. Meaning, entering and bathing are permitted, but eating and drinking with him are forbidden, as stated in Tosefta, chapter 4: it is permitted to enter his house and bathe with him in cold water, but it is forbidden to eat and drink with him. There is a textual error there and the correct reading is "to drink with him in cold water." This is unlike the Rosh and Tur, who permit even eating and drinking because his mouth and heart are not consistent, as stated in chapter 3 of Terumos.

segments.he: בסעודה זו. עבר"נ שם ד"ה תוספתא היה כו' וה"ה כאן:
segments.en: At this meal. See Ran there, s.v. "Tosefta: it was," etc. The same applies here.

segments.he: לאחיו או לבנו. בח"מ סימן שס"ו כתב הטור דין כיוצא בזה לענין גזילה כתב שם דאחיו ר"ל אחי אביו ובניו ר"ל אחיו ורמב"ם לא פירש כן ואין המשנה משמע כדבריו:
segments.en: To his brother or his son. In Choshen Mishpat, siman 366, Tur writes a similar law regarding robbery and explains that "his brother" means his father's brother and "his sons" means his brothers. Rambam does not explain it this way, and the Mishnah does not imply Tur's interpretation.

segments.he: וכן אם פרעם כו'. כ"כ הרמב"ם והטור כתב על זה ואיני מבין את דבריו היאך יהא מותר לו לפרוע חובו מנכסים האסורים עליו הרי הוא נהנה מהם כו' וכתב בית יוסף דאישתמיטתיה לרבינו מתניתין בהגוזל קמא שאמרה בהדיא כמו שכתב הרמב"ם ולענ"ד נראה דשפיר מקשה דעיקר קושיית הטור על מה שכתב הרמב"ם שהנאסר עצמו אומר שפורע חובו בדבר האסור לו ולא אמרו במשנה אלא שהמדיר פורע חוב הנאסר בלי ידיעת הנאסר ורצונו ומה ששנינו במשנה ובאים בע"ח ונפרעים ממנו היינו בעל כרחו שכן משמע הלשון שאמרה המשנה ונפרעים משא"כ בלשון הרמב"ם זה שכתב אם פרעם משמע הוא עצמו והר"ן הביאו ב"י בסי' רי"ו מוקי גם לדברי הרמב"ם אלו באופן זה דאין הוא עצמו משלם לבעל חוב אלא מראה לו מקום היכן הם והטור לא ניחא ליה לפרש בכך. עוד הקשה הטור על מה שכתב הרמב"ם כאן וצריך להודיעם כו' מאי נפקותא מיניה והר"ן שם תירץ דהך הודעה הוא שהוא כמו הפקר כמי שאומר אלו נכסי אבא איני יודע מה אעשה בהם טלו לעצמכם והיינו ג"כ לפי דרכו שפי' דהוא עצמו אינו פורע אבל הטור דמפרש דברי רמב"ם דהוא עצמו פורע על כן הקשה שפיר נמצא לדינא אין מחלוקת דכל שעושה הוא בעצמו הפרעון אסור ולא מהני מה שמודיע אלא שלענין נותן ירושת אביו לבניו סובר הר"ן גם כן דאסור כשהוא נותן בעצמו מפני שיש לו טובת הנאה מזה אלא מיירי שמראה להם מקום ואומר להם נכסים אלו של אבא אסורים עלי איני יודע מה אעשה בהם טלו לעצמכם ותעשו בהם מה שתרצו והב"י כתב שם כיון שמודיעם שממון זה אסור לו ומפני כך נותנו להם והם בניו ואחיו שיש להם שייכות בממון זה הלכך אין לו עליהם טובת הנאה ושרי עד כאן לשונו. ומכל מקום משמע דדוקא דיעבד מהני אם נתן או פרע אבל לא לכתחלה אע"ג שמודיע:
segments.en: "Likewise, if he paid them," etc. Rambam writes this. Tur comments: "I do not understand his words. How can he be permitted to pay his debt from property that is forbidden to him? He is benefiting from it," etc. Beit Yosef writes that Tur overlooked the Mishnah in the first chapter of HaGozel, which explicitly states the law as Rambam rules. In my humble opinion, Tur's question is valid. His principal difficulty is with Rambam's formulation, which implies that the person who is prohibited from benefit himself pays his debt with the forbidden property. The Mishnah says only that the person who imposed the prohibition may pay the other's debt without the prohibited person's knowledge or consent. And when the Mishnah says, "creditors come and collect from it," it means against his will, as the wording "they collect" implies. Rambam's phrase "if he paid them," however, implies that he himself pays. Ran, cited by Beit Yosef in siman 216, likewise interprets Rambam so that the prohibited person does not personally pay his creditor, but merely shows the creditor where the assets are. Tur was unwilling to explain Rambam this way. Tur further asks why Rambam writes here that "he must inform them," for what practical difference does that make? Ran answers that this notification makes the assets comparable to hefker, as though he says, "These are my father's assets; I do not know what to do with them. Take them for yourselves." This answer too follows Ran's approach that the person does not himself make payment. Tur, who understands Rambam to mean that he personally pays, therefore asks properly. Thus there is no practical dispute: whenever he personally makes the payment, it is forbidden, and merely informing the recipients does not help. Regarding giving his father's inheritance to his sons, Ran likewise holds that if he personally gives it to them it is forbidden because he receives the benefit of deciding to whom to give. Rather, he shows them the place and says, "These assets of my father are forbidden to me; I do not know what to do with them. Take them for yourselves and do what you wish." Beit Yosef writes that because he tells them that the money is forbidden to him and for that reason gives it to them, and they are his sons or brothers who have a relationship to this property, he receives no significant benefit from giving it to them and it is permitted. Nevertheless, the language implies that this works only after the fact if he already gave or paid; initially, even if he informs them, it should not be done.

segments.he: אם ישמעו לו. כ"ה הגירסא העיקרית במתני' וער"נ ורא"ש שם:
segments.en: If they will listen to him. This is the primary reading in the Mishnah; see Ran and Rosh there.

segments.he: וזבינא כו'. הרא"ש בפסקיו וטור וכמ"ש בגמ' שם:
segments.en: And I will buy, etc. Rosh in his rulings and Tur, as stated in the Gemara there.

en_segments: If they will listen to him. This is the primary reading in the Mishnah; see Ran and Rosh there.
